extracted.intended_audience: novelists, fiction writers, and critics/students of the craft of fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for novelists on selecting and handling point of view (first/third/omniscient/oblique), and on the relative uses of dramatic (scenic) versus pictorial (narrative/summary) treatment during a book's development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatize the author by placing the storyteller in the story
rubrics_metrics.description: If the story-teller is in the story himself, the author is dramatized; his assertions gain in weight because they are backed by the presence of the narrator in the pictured scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introducing a spokesman or an in-book narrator shifts responsibility from the unseen author to a visible figure, disguises arbitrary authorial voice, and makes the story self-contained. Use this when you want claims to be measured by the reader against a visible observer rather than as naked authorial assertion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present events directly by shifting point of view to enactment
rubrics_metrics.description: Place the reader at the angle of vision so that instead of an account or report, a direct sight of the matter itself is offered while it is passing; the story is enacted rather than narrated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use scenic, enacted presentation when you want immediacy and the sense that the action is occurring as pages are turned. This avoids second-hand reportage and is the method by which fiction moves toward drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserve strict dramatic (scenic) form for subjects that will 'tell themselves'
rubrics_metrics.description: A purely dramatic subject never deviates from a strictly scenic form; one occasion follows another with no reflective summary, and private minds are not directly admitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use strict drama when the story's emphasis is on external action and visible behavior. Do not force dramatic form where the story's main burden lies in inner consciousness, panoramic scope, or where a narrator's reflection is necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pictorial (narrative/omniscient) method for panoramic or interior subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Pictorial books require a narrator (omniscient author or a figure in the book) to gather experience and compose a vision; they are reflective, offering general impressions rather than continuous scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ pictorial narration when the subject demands panoramic survey, long spans of time, or exploration of consciousness that cannot be shown fully in scenes. Accept that this method reports impressions rather than enacting them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer seeing a mind at work (showing consciousness) to retrospective report
rubrics_metrics.description: When the story involves searching exploration of a character's consciousness, an account in his own words after the fact is often inferior to showing him while his mind is actually at work in the agitation that creates the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For inner-life material, strive to render thought-movement and present mental processes (scenic or dramatized interiority) rather than relying solely on retrospective summary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use oblique (third-person-limited) narration to combine character perspective and authorial freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: The author may use a character's field of vision in the third person, keeping the point of view fixed in space but freeing it in time; the author can draw on the serenity of retrospect or the urgency of the present without changing the seen eye.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oblique narration lets you retain a character's bounded vision while gaining temporal flexibility and the ability to supplement that vision with authorial touches (the 'two brains behind the eye'). Use it to deepen depiction without obvious shifts of narrator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blend voices subtly to augment a character's perception
rubrics_metrics.description: In oblique narration there are often touches beyond the character's sensation that indicate another mind is looking over his shoulder — adding richness without blurring focus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ slight authorial augmentation of a character's viewpoint to enrich the picture; keep the blend imperceptible so the focus remains coherent while the scene gains depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of first-person limitations for dramatic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: In first person the narrator's position is fixed and he cannot leave his field of vision; his contribution has a different quality from other people's and cannot achieve the same crispness as direct dramatic presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use first person when the fixed, intimate perspective is essential, but recognize it precludes full dramatic objectivity and may weaken scenes that require unmixed dramatic immediacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow the narrator's consciousness to lapse occasionally to render him objectively
rubrics_metrics.description: An author reporting a first-person seer (by converting to third or oblique narration) can, at suitable moments, close the seer's open consciousness so he becomes impenetrable and stands on the same dramatic plane as other characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intermit a seer's interiority when you want the character to participate as an actor among others rather than as the continuous channel of vision — this helps give him objective weight and avoids his dissolution into an impalpable blur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that a rigid actor-as-narrator forbids 'true' drama
rubrics_metrics.description: A story rigidly told from the point of view of one of the actors denies the full and unmixed effect of drama because one participant's reporting mixes effects and cannot strike with the crispness of direct enactment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid having major dramatic scenes depend solely on one actor's retrospective report; if drama is required, find ways (oblique narration, withdrawal of seer's consciousness, or separate dramatization) to allow the scene to appear unreported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the 'minstrel's licence' (author-as-entertainer) except when justified
rubrics_metrics.description: Telling the story plainly in the author's own voice (minstrel mode) imposes no limitation but is the easiest way and will usually result in a narrower, less disciplined treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve direct authorial narration for rare cases where it loses none of the advantages of more cautious styles; generally prefer methods that make 'the most' of the story by disciplined choice rather than ease.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let the subject dictate the degree of dramatization
rubrics_metrics.description: How far to dramatize versus to use narrative depends entirely on the subject and the effect the theme demands; the subject dictates the method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide the appropriate mix of scene, picture, and narration based on what best serves the theme and the story's aims rather than following a favored technique mechanically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat the scene as the prime dramatic instrument but use it sparingly and prepared
rubrics_metrics.description: The dramatic incident (scene) is first in importance; it is the sharpest effect but expensive in time/space and cannot foreshorten time or cover more than it renders. If wasted or unprepared it loses force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use scenes to clinch matters, demonstrate results, or crown effects already half-made by other means. Prepare scenes in advance and avoid frivolous scenic presentation; a fully wrought scene where every part advances the story is a rare and powerful achievement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use picture (general survey/panorama) to accumulate impression and prepare drama
rubrics_metrics.description: Picture (panoramic narration) handles time and space economy, travels over periods and expanses, and piles up impressions that drama will later complete; it is preliminary and preparatory relative to scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ picture where long reach or breadth is needed and to build material that later dramatization will finalize. Accept that picture is thinner than drama but indispensable for what drama lacks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convert pictorial weakness into strength by dramatizing the narrator's mind
rubrics_metrics.description: The thinness of mere pictorial report can be admitted and emphasized so that the mirror (the narrator's mind) becomes a solid object to be dramatized; by doing this the method's weakness becomes a new kind of strength.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When centering a story in someone's constituted mind, treat the mind itself as dramatic material (the 'mirror') — dramatize reactions, thought-forms, and the mind's processes so that pictorial reportage yields dramatic power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have a working theory of the relative uses of narrative devices
rubrics_metrics.description: A novelist should possess some working theory to guide the relative uses and values of different means (scene, picture, narration) and to decide which to use at what stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop an intentional strategy for how scenes, panoramas, and points of view will be combined across the book. Criticism and study should likewise focus on the technical making of novels by 'reading constructively' to understand craftsmen's choices.
